items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: sitting next to Lester Young — gee whiz, what a thrill you know. Jo Jones. Walter Page. Freddie Green, Buck Clayton, sitting next to him

ctx.x: There’s no rehearsal time to do that. You’re playing every night, right?

Sure, sure. But he encouraged me, and I stayed there for 20 years in and out you know. And had it not been for Count Basie, I wouldn’t be here with you, because nobody would have never heard about me. He gave me a chance and I had so much fun I don’t know why he kept me with the band because I was having a ball. You know every night was fun to me. Just absolutely — sitting next to Lester Young — gee whiz, what a thrill you know. Jo Jones. Walter Page. Freddie Green, Buck Clayton, sitting next to him — you

know it wasn’t but three trumpets, Buck Clayton, Ed Lewis and myself; there was two trombones, and four saxophones. And four rhythm section. So I should have paid him to be in the band because I was having so much fun.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Freddie Green and I, we were walking someplace in Mississippi and they made us get off the sidewalk and walk in the streets.

ctx.x: We left off, Sweets, telling some tales of the road with Count Basie and some of the troubles you got in with police harassment.

Well, not only police, civilian harassment, all kind of harassments. You know, it’s a funny thing, I can’t understand it. White people didn’t want to be bothered with us but they’d come to the dance and stand behind the rope and listen to us play. They’d come to the black dances. They would have to sit upstairs around in the balcony. They would have a rope around the dance hall where the blacks would be dancing and the whites would be looking. And it would be packed, absolutely packed, Ed, those old tobacco…
How did you manage to come through this without a degree of bitterness?

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Freddie Green and I and the trombone player, Ted Donnelly, we met in front of the Theresa (Hotel) one afternoon

ctx.x: That's right. Well, I thought perhaps you, yourself, wanted to.

No, no. In fact, we didn't even know Basie had a small band. Freddie Green and I and the trombone player, Ted Donnelly, we met in front of the Theresa (Hotel) one afternoon and somebody -- somebody not even a musician -- said, man, how come you all are not going to Chicago? I said, "What do you mean?" He said, "Well, Basie just caught a plane going to Chicago to open up in some bar." Not the Carriage Bar, another bar in Chicago. I said, "You've got to be kidding." I couldn't believe it. I said, "He wouldn't do…
